meta.description: No — Henry Ford didn't say it. Quote Investigator traces this saying only to 1981 (educator Jessie Potter); the Ford ascription is spurious.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you always do what you've always done, you'll always get what you've always got'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Henry Ford. The earliest documented use is 1981, by educator Jessie Potter — the Ford credit is a modern invention with no source.

answer.label: Not Henry Ford — a 1980s saying he never said
answer.sourceLine: There is no record of Henry Ford (d. 1947) ever saying or writing this. According to Quote Investigator ↗, the earliest known instance appeared in 1981, spoken by educator Jessie Potter — who is the leading candidate for coining it, though even that remains uncertain. The Ford attribution is described as “spurious.”

source.heading: Where it really comes from
source.excerpt: If you always do what you’ve always done, you always get what you’ve always gotten.
trail: Anchor: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the saying no earlier than 1981, when educator Jessie Potter was quoted using it in the Milwaukee Sentinel.
QI calls the ascription to Henry Ford — who died in 1947 — “spurious,” alongside an equally unsupported credit to motivational speaker Tony Robbins.

The wording is highly variable across early sightings (“…you always get what you’ve always gotten,” “…you’ll always get what you always got”), a hallmark of a folk proverb rather than a single sourced quotation.
This line appears in Wikiquote’s Henry Ford page ↗ in none of its sections — it is not among his sourced, disputed, or even misattributed quotations.
source.excerptNote: The earliest documented wording, attributed to Jessie Potter in 1981; the now-popular “you’ll always get what you’ve always got” is a smoothed later variant. Per Quote Investigator ↗.
source.rightsNote: This is a modern proverb of unsettled authorship. Its earliest documented appearance is a 1981 newspaper paraphrase of remarks by Jessie Potter, but no one has confirmed who coined it or fixed its exact wording in a published, copyrightable work — so no reliable copyright status can be asserted.

author.name: Jessie Potter
author.heading: So who did say it?
author.metaLine: 1926–2010 · American educator on family relationships & human sexuality
author.bio: Jessie Potter was an American educator and counselor who lectured widely on family life, relationships, and human sexuality, and founded a nonprofit institute in the Chicago area. She is the earliest documented user of this saying — quoted in 1981 — and Quote Investigator’s leading candidate for its author, though researchers stop short of crediting her with certainty. Whoever coined it, it was not Henry Ford.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: A punchy line about change and results is exactly the kind of aphorism that drifts toward a famous industrialist. But the paper trail starts decades after Ford’s death.

items.why: Ford died in 1947, but the saying cannot be traced earlier than 1981. Quote Investigator ↗ flatly calls the Ford linkage “spurious,” and it appears in none of the sourced Ford quotations ↗.
The motivational speaker is often tagged as the source, but QI ↗ finds no support for this either — Robbins popularized it, he did not originate it.

Educator Jessie Potter is the earliest documented user (1981) and QI’s leading candidate for authorship, though the saying’s highly variable wording suggests it may already have been circulating as folk wisdom.

misattribution.truthLine: It’s a modern proverb, not a Ford quotation: the earliest evidence is 1981, and the strongest — still tentative — credit goes to educator Jessie Potter, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Ford
lead: Henry Ford is one of the internet’s great quote magnets: any crisp maxim about efficiency, innovation, or getting results tends to be reassigned to him, because he reads as the patron saint of the self-made industrialist. This saying — a neat little loop about doing the same thing and expecting different results — fits that mold perfectly, which is precisely why it should raise suspicion.

In reality the phrase behaves like a proverb: it shows up in the 1980s in several near-identical shapes, none citing a prior author. That variability is the fingerprint of folk wisdom passed mouth to mouth, not a sentence composed by a single famous pen.
context.pull: A quote about results, with no source, drifting toward the most famous plausible name — the classic misattribution pattern.
